installation.note: cp is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: cp (copy) copies files and directories from one location to another. It creates duplicates of the source files/directories at the destination. Unlike mv, cp leaves the original files intact and creates new copies.
when_to_use: Copy files to a different location
Preserve original files while creating copies
Copy files to remote locations (with scp)

misconceptions.title: cp moves files
misconceptions.misconception: cp removes the original file after copying
misconceptions.reality: cp creates a copy while leaving the original intact. Use mv if you want to move (remove original).
misconceptions.tip: cp = copy (keeps original). mv = move (removes original).

misconceptions.title: cp works on directories without -r
misconceptions.misconception: cp directory/ backup/ will copy a directory
misconceptions.reality: You must use -r (recursive) to copy directories. Without it, cp will fail or do nothing.
misconceptions.tip: Always use -r or -R when copying directories: cp -r source/ dest/

misconceptions.title: cp preserves permissions by default
misconceptions.misconception: cp keeps original file permissions automatically
misconceptions.reality: cp doesn't preserve permissions by default. Use -p or -a to preserve permissions, ownership, and timestamps.
misconceptions.tip: Use -p to preserve permissions, or -a for complete preservation (archive mode)

common_pitfalls.description: Trying to copy a directory without the -r flag
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use -r or -R when copying directories. Use -a for complete archive copies. Error message will say 'omitting directory' if you forget.

common_pitfalls.description: cp overwrites existing files without warning by default
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -i for interactive mode (prompts before overwriting) or -n to never overwrite. Or check destination first with ls.

common_pitfalls.description: Mistyping destination path or forgetting trailing slash
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -v (verbose) to see what's being copied. Double-check destination paths. Remember: trailing slash on destination means directory.

common_pitfalls.description: Copied files don't have same permissions as originals
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -p to preserve permissions and ownership, or -a (archive mode) for complete preservation. Note: you may need sudo to preserve ownership.

common_pitfalls.description: Putting files in wrong order (destination before source)
common_pitfalls.solution: Format is always: cp SOURCE DESTINATION. Last argument is always destination. If copying multiple files, last must be a directory.

best_practices: Always use -r or -R when copying directories
Use -i for interactive mode to prevent accidental overwrites
Use -u for syncing - only copies if source is newer
Use -v for verbose output to see what's being copied
Use -a for complete backups to preserve all attributes
Verify destination exists before copying: ls destination/
Use -n to never overwrite existing files
Check copied files with ls after cp to verify success
performance_tips: cp is fast for local file system copies
Use -u to avoid unnecessary copying of unchanged files
For large directories, rsync may be faster than cp -r
cp preserves hard links by default, which can save space
Use -a for complete backups but it's slightly slower due to attribute preservation

additional_notes.copy_vs_move: cp creates copies (original remains). Use mv to move (original is removed).
additional_notes.directory_copying: Always use -r or -R for directories. -a includes -R and preserves everything.
additional_notes.preservation: Default cp doesn't preserve permissions. Use -p or -a for that.
additional_notes.wildcards: cp supports wildcards: cp *.txt dir/ copies all .txt files
additional_notes.multiple_sources: Can copy multiple files: cp file1.txt file2.txt dir/ (destination must be directory)
additional_notes.overwrite_behavior: By default, cp overwrites without asking. Use -i for safety.
